tts: So what do you think of the illuminations? Are you glad we came? — Oh, definitely. It was well worth coming here. What I particularly like is the contrast of old and new: all this modern light and sound technology against the backdrop of the beautiful old buildings.
Yeah, me too. And the colours are just stunning. That projection of the flowers against the town hall was magical.
Yes. And I really like the way the buildings seemed to come alive with the moving images. I think the highlight for me was that building with the giant face projected onto it.
Oh yes, that was pretty dramatic. I found it a bit disturbing, though. — Really? I thought it was brilliant. — Don’t get me wrong, I did too. Just a bit scary. It was so huge, and noisy.
The only thing I’m not so keen on is the crowds. It’s a bit too packed for my liking, especially in the main square.

tts: Tomorrow I think we should come back a bit later, when there are fewer people. There is plenty more to see.
And I would like to see some of the artworks again. The fish in a phone box, for example. — Really? I wasn’t so keen on that one, to be honest. I didn’t really see the point of it.

The point of it is that it is unusual to see fish in a phone box. — Yes, I know, but the reviews said it was one of the highlights of the event, and I just wasn’t that impressed. It didn’t really live up to my expectations. I think I was expecting something a bit more colourful.
Anyway, I am getting really chilly. Shall we go and get a hot drink somewhere?

acts.title: Traditional Skills
tts: In the modern world, China is a major player. It has the world’s second-biggest economy, worth over nine trillion dollars, and dominates manufacturing, producing around ninety per cent of the world’s computers, seventy per cent of the world’s phones and sixty per cent of the world’s shoes.
China is also one of the world’s oldest civilizations. Many of the most important modern inventions happened here, and one of those was the invention of paper.
Paper was first made here in the Han dynasty over two thousand years ago and spread across the world via ancient China’s trading routes.

This is Shiqiao Village in Guizhou province, one of the few places left in China that still makes its living from paper-making using traditional techniques. It was once a centre of the industry, famed for its delicate Xuan paper; today it is mainly a tourist attraction.

It starts with the Wingceltis tree, a variety of elm whose bark is crucial to Xuan paper. The limbs are hacked down and stripped of their bark, which is washed in the local river before being separated into long strands of fibre. The workers here use very little machinery. Instead they use their hands.

acts.title: Traditional Skills
tts: China produces around ninety per cent of the world’s computers and sixty per cent of the world’s shoes.
Paper was first made in China in the Han dynasty over two thousand years ago.

Once the bark has been stripped as finely as possible, it is boiled and steamed in vats heated by large coal ovens. The softened bark is then pounded by large wooden mallets, which separates the fibre.
The pulp is filtered using large wooden screens, and the process is repeated again and again until all the fibre is removed. The sheets are separated and brushed against the wall to dry.

The paper is thicker and more like fabric than mass-produced paper, and it is used to make a range of products, from notebooks to lanterns. It is more expensive, but it is made to be kept rather than discarded.

acts.title: Impressions: what you liked, and what you did not
rule: Giving an impression well is a matter of structure rather than vocabulary. English speakers name what they liked, name the single best part, and then place any reservation carefully — usually softened, and usually after the praise rather than instead of it.
points: What I particularly liked was… This frame front-loads the thing itself, which is why it sounds considered.
I found it a bit… / It was a bit too … for my liking. The a bit does almost all the work.
I wasn’t so keen on… / I didn’t really see the point of it.
It didn’t really live up to my expectations. Note the fixed shape: live up to.
Don’t get me wrong — used before you agree with a criticism you are about to soften.
eg: What I particularly liked was the contrast of old and new.
Front-loads the thing.
The highlight for me was the projection on the town hall.
The single best part.
It was well worth coming.
Overall verdict, positive.
I found it a bit disturbing, though.
Softened reservation, placed after praise.
It’s a bit too packed for my liking.
The standard frame for a crowd complaint.
I wasn’t so keen on that one, to be honest.
Gentle rejection.
I didn’t really see the point of it.
Stronger, but still not rude.
It didn’t really live up to my expectations.
Disappointment, formally correct.
Don’t get me wrong, I liked it too.
Protects the other person’s view.
I was expecting something a bit more colourful.
Explains the disappointment without attacking.
acts.careful: “It didn’t live up my expectations” and “I wasn’t keen of it” are both wrong. The phrases are fixed: live up TO, keen ON.

acts.title: Light Nights, Karaganda · three stars out of five
parts: 1 · what it is, in one line
2 · what works, with a specific example
text: Light Nights runs for eleven evenings in November and turns four streets of the old centre into a projection screen. Entry is free; almost everything else is not.

What works is the contrast. The technology is modern and the buildings are not, and the organizers have been sensible enough to let the second do most of the work. The projection of moving flowers across the front of the old post office, which was built in 1936 and has never looked better, is worth the walk on its own.

The highlight, though, is the face. A twenty-metre portrait is projected onto the side of the theatre and moves in time with the music, and the effect, standing underneath it, is genuinely disturbing in the way the organizers presumably intended.

What does not work is the scale. The main square is far too packed between seven and nine, and the two smaller installations — including a much-reviewed piece involving fish — are lost in the crowd. I could not see the point of the fish, and I suspect nobody else could either.
Go, but go after nine, when the families have gone home. Three stars, and four if they thin the crowd next year.

write.q: Write a review of about 220 words of something you have been to — a concert, an exhibition, a match, a restaurant, a festival. Follow the model: what it is → what works, with a specific example → the single best part → what does not work → the verdict with advice. Use at least two relative clauses and at least one participle clause.
plan: what it is, in one line
write.model:
The Sunday market behind the old bus station runs from six until about one, and everything worth buying has gone by nine.

What works is that it has never been organized. There is no map and no allocation of pitches, so the woman selling honey is next to a man selling car parts, and both have been in the same two metres of ground for eleven years. Anybody arriving expecting a tourist market will be disappointed, which is the point.

The highlight is the far corner, where four or five families sell what they have grown that week. The tomatoes in August, which are grown about forty kilometres away and travel for one hour, are the best I have eaten anywhere.

What does not work is everything after nine. The good stalls pack up, the crowd thickens, and what remains is phone cases and socks. I found it a bit depressing the first time, having arrived at eleven and assumed that was the market.

Go, and go early. Six is not an exaggeration. Take cash, take a bag, and do not expect anybody to be pleased to see you until you have bought something.
